RARP: A Reverse Address Resolution Protocol

How a diskless workstation learns its own IP address from its hardware address.

PROBLEMA diskless machine knows its MAC address but not its IP address.
MECHANISMIt broadcasts an ARP-shaped packet with opcode 3, and a server that holds a MAC-to-IP table answers with opcode 4.
WHY IT FADEDIt needs a server on every network segment and returns only an address, so BOOTP and then DHCP replaced it in practice.

§1Introduction

The Reverse Address Resolution Protocol (RARP) lets a host discover its protocol address, for example its IP address, when it knows only its hardware address. It is the complement of the Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) in RFC 826, which goes the other way and finds a hardware address from a protocol address.

The RFC's problem statement is short: network hosts such as diskless workstations often know only their hardware interface address when they boot, and "there is no standard mechanism" for finding the rest. Like ARP, RARP assumes a broadcast medium such as Ethernet.

Imagine it's the first day at a new school. You know your name, because it is sewn into your jacket, but you don't know your locker number. So you stand in the hallway and shout: "My name is Sam! What's my locker?" The school office has a list of every name and locker, and someone there shouts back: "Sam, you're locker 21." That's RARP. The jacket name is the computer's MAC address, the locker is its IP address, and the office is the RARP server.

§2Motivation

Diskless workstations booted over the network and had no local disk to hold configuration, yet they needed an IP address before they could talk to anyone. The Ethernet address lives in the network card, but the IP address is assigned by an administrator and has no algorithmic relationship to it. Something had to bridge the two, and in 1984 nothing standard did.

The table compares RARP with the other options for getting an address into a machine that has no disk.

A computer with no hard drive has nowhere to write down its own address, so every time it wakes up it has forgotten. It needs someone to ask.

§3Design

The authors list four considerations behind the design. ARP and RARP are different operations. A RARP server must keep a large database, which is hard to hold inside an operating-system kernel. Ease of implementation and little impact on existing hosts matter. And sharing code with existing software is desirable.

The result is a separate protocol at the data-link level that reuses ARP's packet format.

RARP borrows ARP's envelope but puts a different stamp on it, so computers that only know ARP don't get confused.

§4Packet Format

RARP uses exactly the packet format of ARP. For 48-bit Ethernet addresses and 32-bit Internet addresses every packet has hardware type 1, protocol type 2048 (0x0800, the Ethertype of IP), hardware length 6 and protocol length 4. That adds up to 28 bytes. The RFC leaves the RARP Ethertype "still to be assigned"; it was later registered as 0x8035, different from ARP's 0x0806.

In a request (opcode 3) the sender and target hardware address fields both hold the client's own MAC, and both protocol address fields are undefined. In a reply (opcode 4) the target protocol address carries the answer, and the sender fields identify the responder. Switch between request and reply below to see which fields change.

The packet is a form with nine boxes. The question fills in the box for "my name tag" and leaves "my address" blank. The answer fills in that blank.

§5Protocol Operation

RARP adds two opcodes beside ARP's 1 and 2: 3 ("request reverse") and 4 ("reply reverse"). A packet with any other opcode is undefined. As in ARP there are no "not found" or "error" packets, because several servers may be free to answer; a client that hears nothing should time out after a reasonable time.

Step through the exchange below, then put the server behind a router to see why RARP stays on one network segment.

Ask, wait, get an answer, and if nobody answers, ask again later. If the office is in another building, the shout never gets there.

§6Implementation

The RFC's Appendix A sketches two ways to build a server on 4.2BSD Unix. One runs the whole server outside the kernel and needs a way to receive and send raw data-link packets, such as the CMU packet-filter pseudo driver. The other keeps a small cache of database entries in the kernel, filled from the full database kept by a user process through two new ioctls.

Classic Unix servers such as rarpd answer from the ethers(5) file, which maps a MAC address to a host name, and from the hosts file, which maps that name to an IP address. Neither file is part of the RFC; they are common practice. A server is needed on every network segment, because requests do not cross routers.

The helper keeps two lists: one that says which name tag belongs to which computer, and one that says which address belongs to which computer.

§7What replaced it

RARP's limits were its own design: it works only on one broadcast network segment, and it returns just an address. BOOTP (RFC 951) moved the idea onto UDP and IP so it can be relayed between networks, and added a boot file name and extra fields; RFC 1542 clarified it. DHCP (RFC 2131) added leases and a rich set of options. Those became what machines actually use.

RARP itself has never been withdrawn: the RFC Editor's index lists RFC 903 as an Internet Standard (STD 38), so this page says "superseded in practice", not obsolete.

Later helpers could answer from other buildings and could also tell the computer where to find its files. RARP could do neither.

ELI5

A computer that does not know its own address shouts its name tag number into the room, and a helper who keeps a list tells it which address is its own.

WHERE YOU'LL MEET IT TODAY

As an address-assignment mechanism RARP is almost gone, because DHCP does that job. RARP frames do still turn up in one niche: virtualization software such as QEMU/KVM sends a RARP frame after a live migration so that switches relearn which port the virtual machine's MAC address is on. Packet analyzers such as Wireshark and tcpdump still decode RARP, and Linux still defines the ETH_P_RARP constant.

IMPLEMENTATIONS
  • rarpd (BSD, Linux) — User-space RARP server daemons that answer requests from /etc/ethers and /etc/hosts.
  • Wireshark and tcpdump — Both decode RARP frames (EtherType 0x8035).
  • Linux ETH_P_RARP — The EtherType constant for RARP in the kernel headers.
